blocks.text: Why Chrome is a curator's primary tool

Most collections management systems now live on the web. Whether you use Axiell, CatalogIt, or PastPerfect, you likely spend your day in a browser. Using Chrome on your Mac provides a stable environment for these platforms. It handles complex web interfaces better than many alternatives. You can keep your collections database in one tab and your donor management system in another.

Curatorial research involves dozens of open sources. You might have an archival record, a digital asset manager, and a grant application open at once. Use ⌘ + T to open a new tab quickly. Use ⌘ + Option + Right Arrow to cycle through your open tabs. This keeps your focus on the object you are studying rather than searching for your windows.
If you lose track of your work, use ⌘ + Shift + T to reopen the last closed tab. This is helpful when you accidentally close a record you were editing.
blocks.title: Recover lost work

blocks.text: Using Chrome profiles for work and life

Separation is key to sanity. Create a specific Chrome profile for your museum work. This keeps your work bookmarks, history, and logins separate from your personal accounts. Click your profile icon in the top right corner and select Add. Name it after your museum or your department. This prevents your personal search history from cluttering your professional research.

Lazur helps you when you get stuck in complex browser menus. If you need to clear your cache or find a hidden setting, hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask. Lazur will point at the correct menu item on your screen. It saves you from digging through multiple layers of settings pages.
Keyboard shortcuts for high speed research

items: ⌘ + L: Jump to the address bar to type a new URL.
⌘ + F: Find text on the current page to locate specific object IDs.
⌘ + R: Refresh the page if your collections database hangs.
⌘ + W: Close the current tab quickly.
⌘ + 1 through ⌘ + 8: Switch to a specific tab number.

blocks.text: Handling digital assets and large files

Curators often download large image files. Chrome handles these downloads in a separate manager. Press ⌘ + Shift + J to open the downloads page. Here you can see your history and clear old files. If a download fails, this page will show you the exact error. It is better than guessing why a file did not save.

Sometimes a site will not load. This is common with older museum databases. Try clearing the site data for just that one domain. Click the lock icon in the address bar and select Site Settings. From there, you can clear data and reset permissions. This is often faster than clearing your entire browser history.

Do not just dump links into a folder. Use the bookmark bar to keep your most important collections links visible. Press ⌘ + Shift + B to toggle the bar on and off. Organize them by project or by exhibition. This makes your most used tools available with a single click.

faq.question: Can Lazur click buttons in Chrome for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a voice assistant that points and guides. It cannot click buttons or operate your browser, but it can show you exactly where to click.

faq.question: How do I update Chrome on my Mac?
faq.answer: Chrome usually updates automatically. If you need to force an update, click the three dots in the top right, go to Help, and select About Google Chrome.

faq.question: Is it safe to use Chrome for sensitive museum data?
faq.answer: Yes, provided you use strong passwords and keep your browser updated. Use the Google Password Manager to maintain unique, complex passwords for each of your professional accounts.
